utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88/2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, as usual, if you have any problems with interpretation or hearing the proceedings in the language you understand, please stop me and let me know. The appearances, I note Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Ms. Stewart and a new face, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we have -- well, relatively new lawyer, Caitlin Chittenden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome, Ms. Chittenden. Mr. Tolimir, I note Mr. Gajic is present as legal advisor, good afternoon to you, and Mr. Tolimir, of course, is self-represented. This is the 7th Status Conference in this case and the last one was on the 31st of October. I think we're well familiar with the reasons for the conferences by this time. I have a few matters on the agenda from my perspective this afternoon and then, of course, I'll call upon the parties as to any other matters they wish to raise. I wanted to begin with the discussion of the filings that have been made which follow upon the orders I issued at the last Status Conference. Mr. McCloskey, I know that the -- all of the filings are either under seal or confidential but from my perspective, that's in relation to specific contents so that I don't see any difficulty with the matters I want to address in dealing with that in open session unless you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct, it's just the material inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If I could begin, then, in noting that the Prosecution, Mr. Tolimir, has filed the pre-trial brief as well as two motions for the admission of written evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis and a motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts. Now, I'm well aware, Mr. Tolimir, that you have yet to receive any of these filings in a translated form because they are still being translated, they're quite voluminous. So while those translations are pending, obviously I'm not going to set any further dates that flow from the filing of those materials, nor will any of the dates with respect to your responses on the motions run until such time as you receive the translated versions of the material. However, there is one point that I did want to try and raise with you this afternoon, Mr. Tolimir, and that's in relation to the pre-trial brief which the Prosecution has filed. In that brief, they have requested a lengthening or a permission to exceed the word limit for a pre-trial brief. Now, the word limit is normally 15.000 words and the Prosecution's brief is over 55.000 words, 55.879. Now, obviously that is a decision for the Trial Chamber as to whether or not to extend the length of the pre-trial brief, but the reasons given by the Prosecution are that this much more detailed brief in relation to this case, which is quite a complex one, is of benefit to the Trial Chamber in hearing more detail on the Prosecution's position, and I would say as well that drawing from that, they are indicating it would also be of benefit to you to have more detail in the pre-trial brief than less. So what I wanted to discuss with you was whether you are prepared to agree to that increase in the word count and if so, we can dispose of the matter today, and if not, we'll take a different route. But may I hear from you, Mr. Tolimir, firstly on that issue as to whether you would agree to the Prosecution's request for an extension of the pre-trial brief. Mr. Tolimir, if you did want to discuss that with Mr. Gajic, I would allow that, if you wanted to just have a moment to discuss that with him because that might facilitate things. I see both of you nodding, so perhaps, Mr. Gajic, you could speak with Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Tolimir, I'm not hearing you. I'm not receiving translation. I think there might be a problem with your microphone. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. May God help everyone in the courtroom and everyone involved in the work of -- in this case and all cases before the Tribunal, all trials and everybody who is following the trials and may all the trials here end in accordance with his will and may we all be enlightened by his endless wisdom and may we all understand the word of God. Glory be to God for everything that he has given us and he will give us. Madam Judge, I can give you the following answer: I did not receive the pre-trial brief. My legal advisor has not received it yet. I think that it is a large number of words. It's three or four times greater than the number of words that has been set, 15.000 words, and the Pre-trial Judge has to weigh all this when deciding, but I think that this is a really large number of words and we should be given the right to exceed the number of words in our response to their brief. Well, this is my opinion. I can't tell you anything more than that, because I haven't seen the brief and I don't know, I am not familiar with the contents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Well, what I will do, since that's not a clear agreement, is I will wait until you've received the translation of the pre-trial brief as filed and I will allow you seven days -- I'm sorry. Now we appear to have a problem with Mr. Tolimir not receiving interpretation. Could someone check on this, please. I'll try speaking again to see if you're hearing. Mr. Tolimir, are you receiving -- let's try that again. Are you now receiving interpretation in your language? Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. In light of your comments, I will wait until you've received the translation of the pre-trial brief. I hear what you say about your response, your pre-trial brief. So I will wait until you have received that and you will have seven days from the receipt of that, and this will be confirmed in a written order, to provide me with any comments, specific comments on the request of the Prosecution for an extension after having seen the document and after that, I will make a decision on the Prosecution's request. If we could move, then, to -- and I'll just confirm that with reference with the other filings those have been done in accordance with the order that set the time for the Prosecution and I am advised, Mr. Tolimir, that the translations of the pre-trial brief, the two motions, will be done in fairly short order so that you will have all that material within the -- I hope within a month. All right. So I want to move then to a matter which we discussed at the last Status Conference and I wanted to see if we've made any progress, and that was on the question of agreed facts. So perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, you could provide me with any update on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President, we some time ago, came up with -- well, I asked the team to get together a very short, maybe a page and a half, this was on the 8th of February, to provide to General Tolimir to see if -- if as a kind of a test the waters, some very basic facts out of the indictment, and we have been informed by Mr. Gajic that the General would like to be able to understand our pre-trial brief so he can put these facts in context before making his decision which seemed fair enough to us and we have -- we have been seeing with CLSS when the translations may occur and I know they're working on it but that's all we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. McCloskey. Well, that seems like a very reasonable request on the part of you, Mr. Tolimir, so as I say, I am informed that we're looking at a few weeks but -- for the completion of all of that material, the pre-trial brief and the two motions so we're all aware of the heavy burden that CLSS faces so I have been asking questions about the matter as well, the matter of translation. We will then leave the matter but I'm encouraged to hear that at least there have been discussions and progress and, again, I would urge you to continue, particularly once the pre-trial brief is translated, to have -- initiate those discussions again for the reasons that I explained last time. Okay. I don't think, unless there's any comment on that issue from you, Mr. Tolimir, I'll move on. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no comments to make. The Prosecutor represented what happened between him and my legal advisor correctly. I just wanted to say something about the paper where I am asked to confirm the eight counts in the indictment and I consider this to be less than serious exercise because that would mean that I am proving what the Prosecutor has to prove and I would also be denying what I said under oath here, and that is that I'm not guilty. And I am almost asked to accept what the others accepted through various plea agreements and so on and this is unacceptable to me. I cannot agree to us accepting things that have not been considered and areas that I haven't been able to explore through examining the witnesses, and that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tolimir, I think what we'll do, because we're working a bit in the abstract on this, the Prosecution has put forward potential areas for agreement. You want to review the pre-trial brief first. So let's leave the matter until you've had the opportunity to see the pre-trial brief and review it and then look again at what the Prosecution is proposing. I emphasise again that the areas of agreed facts --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not hearing you at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Tolimir. We appear to be challenged by technology this afternoon. I'll try that again. Are you receiving any interpretation? Is there a problem in the booth? Mr. Tolimir, are you receiving interpretation now? Are you hearing me now? I think that part of the problem may be when you do go to turn the microphone on, be careful to watch the channels because you may be switching the channel at the same time to the English, but you're saying no. You're saying that it's just the microphone button.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only press the button that the gentleman just pressed and the only thing I get then is the French interpretation. I don't hear the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: All right. Well, hopefully it's just a glitch that will cease. I was simply explaining, Mr. Tolimir, I heard your comments but let's leave the matter because I think it's premature to discuss what the Prosecution has put forward in terms of agreed facts, given that you would prefer, understandably, to look at the pre-trial brief before we go any further. So we'll leave the matter of proposed agreed facts for now but I would -- as I say, I'm simply encouraging you, once you've had a chance to review the pre-trial brief, that you'll then have further discussions with the Prosecution on this issue. But we'll leave it there for this afternoon. I did want to discuss basically some trial preparations here. I am aiming to have this matter ready for trial by -- certainly by the summer. Whether it can proceed at that time or not is a different issue because of -- there's a number of complex questions, as you all know, that go into the setting of the trial date but in terms of trial preparations, that is my aim. To that end, Mr. Tolimir, I wanted to make sure this afternoon, because once you receive the pre-trial brief in translated form, I am then going to set and it will be before the next Status Conference, I am going to set deadlines that flow from that with respect to material that you are required to file, in particular with respect to any defence of alibi or special defences and your pre-trial brief. So, what I needed to know from you this afternoon is if there are any particular issues in terms of your trial preparations that you want to raise with me, and I'll begin that subject by dealing with a filing that you made on the 10th of February which related to storage space in the UNDU and your access to it, which I appreciate was an important issue for you in terms of trial preparations. You may have seen, although I'm not sure a translation was received, but the Prosecution filed, on the 24th of February, a response to that indicating that they understood your concerns and thought that the matter should be addressed. In the meantime, from inquiries that I made, because I had seen your filing, I am given to understand that this issue may have been resolved by the detention unit and the officials there such that you are now getting the necessary access to your space. I just wanted to make sure and confirm with you that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The detention unit met my request expressed in my submission. I just want to inform you and this Court that I was forced to request this because I was not even allowed to file my documents. And I thought it inappropriate that my activities be made secondary to those of the people who are outside of this trial and that I'm not able to work on my preparation because for a period of time, I had no access to my own archives. I was only allowed to go in and go out. I want a fair solution; namely, that I have access whenever I'm free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And I'm understanding from your comments that that has now been resolved with the detention unit and that that access is available to you; is that correct? Do you need me to repeat that? I'm understanding from your comments that that has now ... Perhaps you'll have to remain for a moment or two. I'm understanding from your comments that that has now been resolved with the detention unit and that access is available to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, right. Thank you. Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. So then in terms of trial preparations, Mr. Tolimir, as I say, you will be receiving a Scheduling Order that's going to set deadlines for you in terms of your filings, and I just want to make sure that there's no other issues you want to raise at this time about your trial preparations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have to raise an issue that you are already aware of. I'm really in a very unfavourable position because every half hour, I am awakened and checked on, like before, which exhausts me psychologically and mentally because I don't get any uninterrupted sleep longer than 30 minutes. I must ask you to deal with this. I can't believe that you have no way of influencing this because I'll be completely exhausted by the time trial starts. I won't be able to participate. I have to satisfy my bodily need for sleep. That's one issue. The second issue. I'm not allowed to use the teas that I had used before and that I need and I've written about this in my submission. The doctor who visited me in the detention unit even claims it's forbidden, banned in Holland, in detention because by rules of establishment, we get English tea here. Why wouldn't I be able to have tea from Serbia? Please deal with this issue because that only goes to my detriment. I've been here for two years without any inspection or medicine. This is commercially-available tea that you can buy over the counter. It's issued -- it's available from infirmaries, although it's alternative medicine, admittedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. On the first issue that you raise, certainly after the last Status Conference it was a matter of concern to me and I understood the point that you were making. Since then, I've had discussions with the Registrar, with the UNDU on this issue, and I am very hopeful that we are very close to a technological solution to this problem. I understand that that is the situation. The registry is unable to confirm to me yet that the situation will change or has changed, but I understand that they are working on it. They, too, have taken the matter seriously and are working on it and I would encourage you to discuss the matter again with the head of the detention unit, and I will continue to monitor the situation, because as I understand -- I understand that we are going to see a change shortly in that respect. So I do understand the concerns you have raised on this issue. I understand that the detention unit is doing their very best to ensure that the checks that are going on at the moment are not disturbing you, but as I say, in the long term, we're hoping that there's another solution for this problem. So, I would ask you to again, when you go back to the detention unit, to discuss this matter with the authorities at the detention unit and hopefully very soon, we hope to have a resolution of the problem. With reference to the tea. Mr. Tolimir, I do believe it's important. I understand the concerns you've raised about it but I do believe we need to move to the very significant issues that you have to face in terms of preparing for trial. So I'm simply communicating, once again, to the Registry that I really want to see a solution to this problem and I don't want to hear this again at the next Status Conference. That's a message going to both parties. I am sure that there is a way to solve this problem and I would ask the Registrar to convey my concerns back to the UNDU, and I'm hoping that this is the last time we have to discuss that question. And again, please raise this again with the detention unit and I'm hoping, as I say, that this is the last time that particular issue -- I have had discussions on that issue as well and I'm hoping that the matter can simply end here. So those are the -- that's the situation with respect to those two ongoing concerns, Mr. Tolimir. I take it, then, from your comments that there's no other particular points. I wanted to simply point out to you that, as I say, you are now going to be receiving specific filing deadlines and we're coming to a critical time, Mr. Tolimir. I know you don't want to hear this again but I'm going to say it again. You're now at a point where you're going to have to work with a large amount of material and try and start putting some of it into form, for example, in terms of your pre-trial brief, by virtue of your election of self-representation, particularly because you are not a lawyer by training, you are depriving yourself of the full assistance that counsel could give you in that process. I appreciate you have legal advisors. Their role is much, much more limited than full counsel. So I'm not going to discuss the issue with you, I know your position on it. I simply wanted to reiterate that especially now when you're going to have a very short period before I'm going to say in essence to the relevant individuals that this case is ready for trial, I ask you again to think your situation vis-a-vis counsel. But unless, Mr. McCloskey, you have anything to say on pre-trial preparations or materials, I think that's all I wanted to mention on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It may be an issue you were going to ask us about but I know the team that is working on the -- well, what we know are the abbreviated witness testimonies under Rule 92 ter, the unavailable or dead witnesses under 92 quater and the expert reports under 94 bis. We hope to have all that -- those motions filed within the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. McCloskey. It was indeed another issue that I was just going to check on so I'm happy to hear that that material will be forthcoming as well, because obviously that's important for the pre-trial preparations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we were able to give Mr. Gajic today CDs of the index of our 65 ter lists that are hyperlinked to the documents so that should be a very convenient thing for them to have and we are assembling some documents for a motion to add to our 65 ter list, as we will be doing throughout, but the vast majority of them are on those CDs and they are hyperlinked to the original, many times Serbian, documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you for that. If I could just add, I understand on this, the provision of material issue, that the annexes to the 65 ter list, the specific witness lists, the exhibit lists, those have been translated and are about to be provided so that those will be of assistance to you in the preparation process, so my understanding is that material will be available very shortly. Okay. Mr. Tolimir, any other comments on the -- just on the issue of any pre-trial -- your preparations for the trial process?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I have something to say. I think it is wrongly understood that I want time given to me for preparation, time which I ask by being able to have uninterrupted sleep. You say talk to the doctors. The doctors say the Registrar wants to know when you are going to die. I think that's morbid. Only God knows when I will die. I think this is frivolous. My room is equipped with cameras, stereo sound equipment and they still continue to wake me up every 30 minutes. This is physically and mentally exhausting. I think you should view that from the viewpoint of enabling me to work. I don't know why they are checking on me. Until I am found guilty, I am presumed innocent. I don't know why you look at it that way. To achieve something, I get up -- I go to bed at 12.30, after midnight, and wake up at 5.30. Whenever I manage to have a nap during the day, I take the opportunity but you have to give me uninterrupted sleep time because this is really exhausting. I don't know why they are mistreating me in this way, both in terms of sleep and deprivation of my tea. I want to be fully alert. I want to read all the materials and I want to know everything that pertains to me and the Prosecution's case against me. I really want you to create conditions for me to be able to work and to defend myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Let me be very clear here. I do understand the point that you have been raising with regard to your sleep. I did take it very seriously. I do take it very seriously. But the reality is that the officials at the UNDU are the ones who have the hands-on responsibility for your welfare, along with the medical staff, and they are of the opinion, an opinion which I, from a distance, am not prepared to interfere with, as to what steps they must take in order for your welfare. So everyone is well aware of the issue and certainly I understand the point you've raised. What I'm saying to you is not that I'm just ignoring the issue. What I'm saying to you is that I've had discussions. I'm being assured that they're working on an arrangement that will be more suitable for you in terms of interruption of sleep. So I'm simply asking that you give this a bit more time and I'm confident that we're going to resolve the issue. So it's not that I -- that I don't understand the effect on your health or why that's a trial preparation issue. I do, certainly. So for today, all I'm saying is I think we're very close to finding a solution to this problem. I am interested in the problem and I will continue to review it with the Registrar should I not see any movement on the point. So, having dealt then with those issues, and I hope you will take away my words about representation, Mr. Tolimir, I had -- I don't believe I had any other issues to raise this afternoon other than -- which is always my final question to you on health issues. But before I do that, Mr. McCloskey, was there anything else that you wanted to raise this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Madam President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, is there anything else that you wanted to raise and in particular, we've just discussed conditions at the detention unit so I don't think we need to go further on that but if there's anything, any other issues you wanted to raise or anything relating to your health aside from -- we've fully discussed the sleep issue. Anything else you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I want to add something and please do not close the Status Conference yet. There is no reason to adjourn. I want to say just a few sentences. I am in good health and perfectly able and I have lived here for two years without any medicine. In that respect, I am in better health than all those who are taking medication. I just can't understand why I am not able to use health food and tea because I treat myself with prayer. Please understand that. I don't want to be punished by all sorts of censorship and interruption of sleep. Please enable me to have that because I am free here until I am convicted. Please do not impose limitations on me as upon a convict. I am free in every sense except not being able to walk out of the detention unit, but I am free to choose what I'm going to eat or drink. The doctor tells me tea is not allowed in Holland. I'm surprised. If this is a royal country and it bans all the other countries allowed, it's an oddity. I can't understand that we are able to receive tea from England or from other countries, I can't understand why I'm not allowed to get tea from Serbia that I have been drinking for 30 years. However, despite all this, I am feeling great. And every time they keep controlling me, look at the log-book of the guards, they check on me every 30 minutes. I never get up later than 6.30. I spend all my time working on the case. I want to prepare a serious defence. I am in great health, otherwise. Just please don't impose those limitations on me and I don't want to be subjected to any exhausting procedures that disable me. All I want is to prepare and work on this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. I think your -- you've made your position on this very clear and as I say, the Registry, the UNDU and I am well aware of the situation so let's hope that we can resolve these issues shortly. Unless anyone has any other matters to raise, which I'm not seeing any indication of, I believe we can conclude the Status Conference at this time. Okay. Thank you, everyone. Have a good afternoon. We are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
